result.summary: Apollo seeks priests for his Pytho shrine and hijacks a Cretan ship by leaping aboard as a dolphin. He steers it around the Peloponnese to Crisa, appears to the crew as a young man, and tells them they will serve his temple and worship him as Apollo Delphinius.

scenes.title: Apollo seizes the Cretan ship
scenes.summary: Apollo spots a Cretan ship bound for Pylos and leaps aboard as a dolphin. The terrified crew sit silent as the ship shakes.
scenes.stakes: The Cretan sailors fear the monster and the loss of their ship and voyage.

scenes.title: Voyage around the Peloponnese
scenes.summary: The ship, guided by Apollo, passes Malea, Taenarum, Pylos and Elis, sights Ithaca, then turns east up the gulf to Crisa.
scenes.stakes: The crew lose control of their ship and cannot reach the shore they want.

scenes.title: Apollo blazes forth at Crisa
scenes.summary: Apollo leaps out like a star, lights a flame in his shrine, terrifies the Crisaean women, then returns to the ship as a young man.
scenes.stakes: The Crisaeans are frightened by the god's blazing radiance.

scenes.title: Apollo questions the Cretans
scenes.summary: Disguised as a youth, Apollo asks who they are. Their captain answers, praises his godlike look, and asks where they are.
scenes.stakes: The Cretans want to know where they are and hope to return home.

scenes.title: Apollo names them his priests
scenes.summary: Apollo reveals himself, says they will never return home but will keep his temple, and instructs them to build an altar and honour him as Delphinius.
scenes.stakes: The Cretans must give up their homes and families to serve the god.

alias_notes.explanation: Cult title from delphis, Greek for dolphin, recalling his dolphin form.
Common epithet of Apollo, meaning bright.

notable_quotes.reason: Vivid image of Apollo leaping from the ship like a star at noon.
Explains the origin of the cult title Delphinius.

analysis.text: The god's power over mortals is shown as he redirects the sailors' course and their lives to serve his purposes.
The passage gives an aetiology for Delphi, linking its priesthood to Cretan origins and explaining the name Delphi and cult title Delphinius.

legacy.text: The dolphin became associated with Apollo and Delphi, and the story offered a folk explanation for the name Delphi.

fun_facts.text: The paean cry Ie Paean in the hymn became the name of a type of Greek hymn to Apollo.

language_notes.text: "Wine-like sea" renders a Homeric epithet for the sea's deep, dark colour, not its taste.
"Gave heed so as to understand" means the crew did not realise the dolphin was a god.
"Sheets" are the ropes controlling the sail, not cloth; the crew leave them untouched.
"Sea-garlanded" means encircled by the sea, describing Taenarum on its headland.
A catalogue of Peloponnesian coastal places, tracing the ship's route past Pylos and Elis, where the Epei lived.
"By ordinance of Zeus" means the wind came by Zeus's decree, serving Apollo's plan.
"Like a star at noonday" pictures a blazing light visible even in full daylight, signalling the god's divine epiphany.
"Winged words" is a Homeric formula for words that fly swiftly from speaker to listener.
"Traffic" means trade or commerce; the god asks whether they are merchants or pirates.
"Men who live by bread" means ordinary mortals, who must eat, in contrast to the gods.
Pylos is a city in the south-western Peloponnese; the Cretans were sailing there for trade, but were driven off course to Crisa.
Delphinius comes from Greek delphis, "dolphin"; Apollo took dolphin form to lead the ship, explaining the cult title and a link to Delphi.
"Overlooking[2512]" is a textual corruption or editorial footnote marker; the original wording is uncertain.
"Ie Paean" is a ritual cry to Apollo as healer, sung in processions and thanksgiving.

context_notes.text: Cnossos was the chief city of Crete, linked with king Minos. Apollo's later priests at Delphi are to come from these Cretans.
Helios is the sun god. His sacred sheep were said to graze at Taenarum, the southern tip of the Peloponnese.
Ithaca, Dulichium, Same and Zacynthus are islands in the Ionian Sea off western Greece.
Crisa lay near Delphi on the Corinthian gulf; it was the port from which pilgrims approached Pytho.
Tripods were bronze cauldrons on three legs, valuable dedications in Greek shrines and closely associated with Apollo's oracle.
Long uncut hair was typical of young Greek men and of Apollo, who was usually shown as an unshorn youth.
Cnossos was the great Cretan city associated with King Minos. The sailors are told they will become Apollo's temple servants.
Offering white meal (barley meal) was a simple, common sacrifice, here establishing the cult's first altar.

literary_notes.text: Apollo's transformation into a dolphin shows divine power disguised as a frightening animal, as part of his plan.
Repeated 'black' and 'hollow' ship details, with silent men and unchanged sails, build a tense, eerie stillness.
The ship ignores the helm because the crew think they steer it, while Apollo, the unseen god, controls it.
Apollo's leap is compared to a star, conveying his brilliance and the sudden, awe-inspiring revelation of his divinity.
"Swift as a thought" stresses the god's effortless speed; mortals cannot match the immediacy of divine movement.
The captain notices the stranger looks godlike and does not realise he is actually speaking to the god who led them.
The Cretans blame "one of the deathless gods" for their course, unaware that the god is the youth before them.
